title: Sisney v. Reisch
summary: An inmate sufficiently alleged a right to enforce a settlement promising certified kosher meals to all Jewish inmates who requested them; dismissal was reversed.
notes: The edited opinion does not reproduce the full immunity analysis. Its reported conclusion is retained without reconstructing omitted reasoning. The editors emphasize that available relief can differ with the defendants and their immunity positions.

sections.Parties: Charles Sisney was the inmate seeking enforcement. Tim Reisch, the Secretary of Corrections, and Douglas Weber, the prison-operations director, were the officials sued. The underlying settlement had been signed by a former secretary and another inmate, Philip Heftel.
sections.Material Facts:
Heftel had brought a federal civil-rights action alleging interference with his Jewish religious practice. The 2000 settlement expressly promised a kosher diet to all Jewish inmates who requested it, including prepackaged certified kosher meals at noon and in the evening. In 2007 the provider stopped supplying those meals and substituted food prepared in the prison kitchen. Sisney alleged that the new diet violated both the settlement and his religious practice. His grievance was rejected because he was not an original party to the settlement.

Sisney’s complaint identified the defendants’ official responsibilities and the predecessor secretary’s execution of the agreement. Unlike the general food-service contract in Sisney v. State, this agreement expressly identified a class of intended recipients and repeatedly promised specified benefits to that class.
sections.Procedural History: The circuit court dismissed for insufficient allegations about the officials’ responsibilities and statutory immunity, without deciding beneficiary status. The South Dakota Supreme Court reversed and remanded in 2008. It found the allegations sufficient to support officials’ responsibility, beneficiary status, and the contract action’s survival of the asserted immunity obstacle.
sections.Issue: Could an inmate who did not sign the settlement state a third-party-beneficiary claim by alleging membership in the expressly protected class?
sections.Holding: Yes. The settlement’s language and Sisney’s alleged membership in the class sufficiently supported an intended-beneficiary claim at the pleading stage. The court did not enter a final damages judgment or decide every disputed fact.
sections.Reasoning:
The beneficiary statute requires a clear intent to benefit the claimant, but the claimant need not be named individually if the contract identifies a class to which he belongs. A promise to all Jewish inmates requesting kosher meals supplied that identification. The detailed requirements about meal content and delivery reinforced the inference of a direct intended benefit.

The officials’ roles also supported an inference that they were responsible for carrying out a departmental settlement signed by their predecessor. At this procedural stage Sisney was entitled to favorable inferences from his allegations. The court therefore rejected dismissal and allowed the enforcement claim to proceed. This reasoning turns on the settlement’s actual language and the pleading standard, which must remain distinct from a final adjudication of breach.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: Together the two Sisney decisions isolate the importance of identifying the precise contract, its beneficiaries, the defendant’s duty, and the procedural posture.

topics.third-party-beneficiaries: Recognizes a sufficiently identified class of intended recipients at the pleading stage.
topics.interpretation: Uses express class-benefit language to distinguish the general food-service contract.
topics.public-contracts: Allows this settlement-based claim despite the restrictive result in the companion public-contract case.

mnemonic.rationale: The same prisoner, the second claim
